title: In Katrina's wake, one New Orleans community thrives as another still fights for survival - NewsBreak
text:
By Rick Jervis ,
37 minutes ago
NEW ORLEANS – It’s breakfast time at the Hey! Café in this city’s Broadmoor neighborhood, and patrons line up to buy steaming cups of cafe au lait and freshly baked biscuit breakfast sandwiches. Some peck away at laptops. Others read books within its brightly colored walls with shelves selling branded caps and mugs.
On a recent weekday morning, there was little – if any – reminder of the floodwaters that, two decades ago, had muscled their way into the streets outside, invading homes and wrecking businesses.
Few reminders of the devastation and heartbreak.
Seven miles upriver, in the Lower Ninth Ward, concrete steps still stand sentry over empty lots, their houses long washed away. Overgrown lots outnumber grocery stores. And streets, once filled with the sounds of children playing or locals playing dominoes, are mostly quiet, punctured occasionally by the sound of a distant lawn mower.
Harry Sims, 72, Lower Ninth Ward resident, helped rescue several people on his skiff during the floods. Built a new home on Flood Street using federal recovery funds, but there are empty lots all around him. "You can't run from home," he says. By Jack Gruber, Jack Gruber-USA TODAY “Wasn’t always like this,” said Harry Sims, 72, whose house, on aptly-named Flood Street, is ringed on three sides by empty lots. “Katrina chased them all away.”
It’s been 20 years since Hurricane Katrina roared ashore on the Gulf Coast on the morning of Aug. 29, 2005, and the federal levees failed across New Orleans, unleashing flood torrents across the city.
The Category 3 hurricane and the ensuing breached levees and floodwalls caused more than 1,300 deaths – many of them in the Lower Ninth Ward – and around $200 billion in undefined (adjusted for inflation), making it at the time the costliest hurricane ever to hit the USA. The disaster still claims the third-highest death toll from a hurricane in recorded U.S. history, according to federal estimates.
Though Katrina also devastated Alabama, Mississippi and other parts of Louisiana, New Orleans received the lion’s share of damage: Around 80% of the city was underwater for weeks, and the city lost more than 120,000 of its residents, who fled from the storm and never returned.
Areas of the Ninth Ward in New Orleans are still flooded after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita on September 26, 2005. By ROBYN BECK, AFP via Getty Images The storm also redrew the city’s racial makeup: New Orleans today is less Black and more Latino, with many more out-of-town residents, many of whom were part of a wave of volunteers that descended into the city to help rebuild, then stayed.
“I was devastated,” Cotlon, 58, remembered. “It hurt.”
The percentage of Black residents in New Orleans, though still the majority, dropped from 67% in 2000 to 56% in 2024, according to The Data Center, which tracks New Orleans’ population figures. At the same time, the city added more than 15,000 Hispanic residents.
Today, visitors to New Orleans may spend days in the city without ever knowing it endured such a catastrophe. The French Quarter and most of Uptown and the Garden District hum with music halls and busy white-tableclothed eateries. The city’s iconic Superdome – which sheltered some 20,000 people during Katrina and the ensuing floods and became a symbol of the city’s misery – has hosted two Super Bowls and two Final Four college basketball games since the storm.
But venture outside of the tourist areas and scars from the flood begin to emerge.
Empty lots line streets from Gentilly to the Lower Ninth Ward. Flood-scarred homes dot the city. Some neighborhoods lack basic needs, like schools and health clinics.
“We're far from 100%,” longtime musician and resident John Boutte said. “There are still neighborhoods you go through and there are houses that have not been touched since the storm.”
At a cost of $14.5 billion, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has substantially rebuilt and bolstered the area’s defenses to prevent another Katrina-like flood, though some experts warn that, without rebuilding depleted coastal wetlands to act as a buffer, a direct hit from a future storm could again submerge the city, parts of which sit below sea level.
How did Katrina and the ensuing floods substantially redefine New Orleans? Depends where in the city one asks.
Broadmoor and the Lower Ninth Ward tell competing stories of the storm. Both were home to many of the city’s Black residents, both had unique histories and social makeups, and both were walloped with walls of floodwater.
Yet, one emerged and rebuilt stronger than before. The other remains entrenched in a battle for survival.
Picking through mud-caked debris Burnell Cotlon remembers walking through the ruins of his Lower Ninth Ward home a few weeks after Katrina. Sun-baked mud covered most of the neighborhood. Houses sat in splintered ruins, as if blown up by dynamite.
Others had simply vanished, washed away someplace else. A large section of the 6-foot-high concrete wall lining the Industrial Canal on the outer edge of the Lower Ninth lay twisted on the ground – the gash that let the floodwaters in, trapping families in attics and on roofs and drowning many others.
Burnell Cotlon, owner of Burnell's Lower 9th Ward Market, started the first - and only - grocery store in the Lower Ninth Ward following Katrina's floods. By Jack Gruber, USA TODAY Floodwaters pushed Cotlon’s double shotgun home on Tricou Street off its foundation and delivered it in ruins to the middle of the street. On that hot September day, he had picked through the mud-caked debris: Moldy clothes. Splintered furniture. A mildewy photo album containing the only family pictures of his grandparents. The album disintegrated as he picked it up. He buried his hands in his face and cried.
Born and raised in the Lower Ninth Ward, Cotlon had joined the U.S. Army and served as a military policeman in Germany for several years before returning to his hometown. He married his wife, Keasha, and bought the home on Tricou Street in 2001 using a VA home loan.
In Katrina’s aftermath, Cotlon had to make a choice faced by thousands of other New Orleanians: Stay in a neighborhood thoroughly devastated by floods? Or relocate?
Cotlon and his wife stayed.
One day in the months following Katrina, as he was mowing the lawn on his property, an elderly lady known in the neighborhood simply as Ms. Emmanuelle exited a taxi pulling several bags of groceries with her. She told him she had to take a taxi several miles downriver to New Orleans East to get groceries.
“There was nothing: No hospitals, no stores, no nothing at all,” Cotlon said. “I said, ‘This is crazy. I have to fix this.’”
He used his savings to buy a squat, 6,000-square-foot brick building on Fats Domino Avenue, named after the storied musician who was rescued from his home down the street, which had been abandoned after the floods. He fixed up the building, added shelving and paid for permits.
Today, Cotlon runs Burnell’s Lower 9th Ward Market, the sole grocery store in the neighborhood and the only one for miles selling staples like bananas, fresh bread and eggs. Loaves of bread, rice, beans, pasta, rolls of toilet paper, diapers, shaving cream and boxes of Zatarain’s Crawfish, Shrimp & Crab Boil seasoning line the shelves. Customers shuffle in and pay in crumpled bills or promises. His wife keeps tabs on an iPad on who owes them money.
Burnell Cotlon, owner of Burnell's Lower 9th Ward Market, started the first - and only - grocery store in the Lower Ninth Ward following Katrina's floods. By Jack Gruber, USA TODAY Cotlon initially opened the store three days a week but expanded to seven, hoping to help jump-start recovery in his neighborhood. But the process has been slow and arduous. Cotlon once knew the names of all 30 of his neighbors. Today, there are only four.
“The people say they're not coming back because there's not enough stores, and the stores are not coming back because there’s not enough people,” he said. “Meanwhile, the people that are there are suffering. For now, it’s just me.”
‘People just didn’t have a chance’ The floods in Katrina’s wake hit the Lower Ninth Ward with the force of several runaway trains. As the federally engineered floodwalls collapsed, walls of water rushed into the neighborhood from multiple sides, crushing homes or sweeping them off their lots.
Hundreds of residents drowned. Most survivors fled and started lives in other cities across the United States. The neighborhood’s population dropped by nearly two-thirds after the floods, from 14,000 pre-Katrina to 5,095 in 2023, according to The Data Center.
The number of households also plummeted, from 4,820 pre-Katrina to 1,883 in 2020, leaving a barren landscape of empty lots and abandoned homes. The exodus has altered the city’s racial makeup: Pre-Katrina, the Lower Ninth Ward was 98% Black, 0.5% White and 0.5% Hispanic; today it’s 90% Black, 5% White and 2.6% Hispanic.
Though the majority of Lower Ninth residents were homeowners – around 55% owned their homes, a percentage that easily outpaced the city average – they also tended to be low income and uninsured, leading to rebuilding challenges, said Laura Paul, executive director of Lowernine.org, a nonprofit aimed at rebuilding the neighborhood.
Laura Paul, executive director of lowernine.org, a nonprofit created after the floods to help residents return to the Lower Ninth Ward, standing on the porch of the food pantry headquarters along the Industrial Canal which breached flooding the Lower Ninth Ward following Hurricane Katrina. Her group has built 98 homes for residents and done repairs or renovations on 400 other properties. By Jack Gruber, USA TODAY Paul, originally from Montreal, arrived in New Orleans in early 2006 and focused her energy on helping the Lower Ninth recover. She quickly noticed residents there – and evacuees trying to return – were falling through the cracks, she said.
Initiatives like the Road Home Program, where the state distributed federal funds to help Katrina victims, discriminated against the Lower Ninth’s mostly Black residents, she said, because it awarded grants based on either pre-storm values of homes or the estimated cost of repairs – whichever was lower. The low values of Lower Ninth homes meant residents weren’t getting enough to rebuild.
Housing advocates sued and, in 2010, a U.S. District Court judge found the formula discriminatory, declaring that, “on average, African-American homeowners received awards that fell farther short of the cost of repairing their homes than did white recipients.”
The Make It Right Foundation, the Brad Pitt-led effort to build affordable homes in the Lower Ninth Ward, was once heralded as a post-Katrina feel-good story. But many of the 109 homes built through the initiative have not weathered the southern Louisiana heat and humidity well, giving way to rot, mold and structural defects, according to a 2018 class-action lawsuit brought by the homeowners.
Paul said more homes could have been built better with less money. So far, her group has built 98 homes in the Lower Ninth Ward and helped with repair or renovations to more than 400 properties, she said. Much more is needed.
“You take a low-wealth community, you throw a disaster like that at them, and then you follow it up with a federally funded, state-administered program that's found to be discriminatory in a federal court,” she said. “People just didn't have a chance, honestly.”
‘All these years, it still hurts’ Sims, the Flood Street resident, said he rode out the floods at his home and then climbed into a skiff and helped evacuate stranded neighbors. While others fled the city, he stayed in a temporary trailer in Uptown, working as a long shoreman to help clear debris.
Then he returned to the Lower Ninth Ward. His house was ruined. His neighbors were gone. But he used federal disaster funds to buy a new home that’s closer to the levees but better elevated and more resistant to future floods.
A church in Harahan donated an outdoor boxing ring that he set up in the empty lot next door. His plan is to train local kids and keep them out of trouble. Lately, though, the ring has been pretty quiet.
Sims said he misses the sound of children outside and the evening dominoes games he had with neighbors. Still, he plans to stay.
“Disasters are everywhere. You can't hide,” he said. “You just have to be prepared and know how to help each other.”
There’s another reason he stayed.
“I wouldn't leave because I don't want to know no other culture,” he said. “Because I come up in it, and I know it.”
On a recent afternoon, Cotlon pulled grocery items from the shelves of his market, stuffed them into empty plastic Walmart bags and climbed into his Ford C-Max. A few days a week, he drives the groceries to customers too old or too frail to make it to the store. Some, like Ms. Emmanuelle, pay ahead. Others pay at the end of the month, when Social Security or disability checks come in.
Harry Sims, 72, Lower Ninth Ward resident, helped rescue several people on his skiff during the floods. Built a new home on Flood Street using federal recovery funds, but there are empty lots all around him. "You can't run from home," he says. By Jack Gruber, USA TODAY “How you feeling?” Cotlon called out as he walked a plastic bag filled with laundry detergent and flea spray to the front door of a customer known as “Big Bruce.”
Cotlon asked him if he’d been keeping up with his exercises to ease a herniated disc. Big Bruce said he was.
“That’s what I’m talking about,” Cotlon said, smiling. “Tell your family I say hello.”
Cotlon said he’ll continue stocking his shelves and driving over groceries for as long as residents need. But he feels more people would move back to the Lower Ninth Ward if there were more affordable housing options.
Since Katrina, he’s been buying up empty lots around the neighborhood and would love to develop affordable homes on them. But it’s a dream that revenue from a local market alone can’t fund.
Cotlon has garnered widespread praise for his quixotic efforts in the Lower Ninth Ward, including writeups in national newspapers, visits by luminaries like Mark Zuckerberg and rapper T.I. and an appearance on the “Ellen DeGeneres Show.” (DeGeneres donated five washer/dryer sets, which allowed Cotlon to open a small laundromat next to the market; she also donated Cotlon’s C-Max.)
Despite all the attention, Cotlon said the Lower Ninth remains unbuilt. The empty lots, he said, are a searing reminder of how much work there’s left to do.
“When I drive from my home to the store, I remember what used to be a school. I remember what used to be a clinic,” he said. “It still hurts, you know. All these years later, it still hurts.”
‘Something we had never seen before’ Unlike the walls of water that barreled into the Lower Ninth Ward, the floods snuck into Broadmoor, seeping down streets and creeping into homes – slowly, steadily – until nearly the entire neighborhood was submerged.
Sinnidra Taylor, 41, was a senior at Xavier University and living with her family in their Broadmoor home when they evacuated from Katrina. After the storm passed, they returned home, and she and other residents organized a crawfish boil to feed residents who were still there.
Then the water returned.
Sinnidra Taylor, a Broadmoor native and owner of Crazy Waffle Bar, was one of the first Broadmoor residents to return after the floods and later founded Friends of Cody's NOLA, in 2020. By Jack Gruber, Jack Gruber-USA TODAY During the outdoor cookout, Taylor said she could see water rolling down streets and seeping into yards. By the time she and her family gathered their things and walked back outside, water was up to her neck, she said.
The destruction of the nearby floodwalls and levees had pushed water into the lowest parts of the city. More than 5 feet of water had invaded Broadmoor. Taylor and her family evacuated again.
“You could imagine how terrifying it was,” Taylor remembered. “The hurricane had passed. And then we see water rushing up the street. That was something we had never seen before.”
Located in New Orleans’ Uptown area, Broadmoor is one of the city’s lowest-lying areas. It was a boggy marsh until the city’s pumps began draining water from New Orleans around the 1920s, said Richard Campanella, a professor of geography and associate dean for research at the Tulane University School of Architecture and Built Environment, who has studied New Orleans’ neighborhoods post-Katrina.
Even the neighborhood’s name – “broad moor” – depicts early city leaders’ defiance in reclaiming this swampy part of the city, he said.
“Broadmoor was about five miles upriver of the original city, entirely on lower ground,” Campanella said, “and was partly African-American and partly White and split in terms of class as well.”
Sinnidra Taylor, right, a Broadmoor native and owner of Crazy Waffle Bar, was one of the first Broadmoor residents to return after the floods and later founded Friends of Cody's NOLA, in 2020, New Orleans' first shared kitchen incubator, a nonprofit focused on access to affordable commercial kitchen space, technical assistance and revenue generating opportunities for New Orleans food entrepreneurs. By Jack Gruber, USA TODAY By the 1950s and 1960s, Broadmoor was one of the most racially and economically diverse pockets of the city. Future political leaders grew up playing alongside the children of teachers and waiters. Former Mayor Mitch Landrieu and his sister, former Democratic U.S. Sen. Mary Landrieu, were raised in a house on Prieur Street. Walter Isaacson, former Time magazine editor and biographer of people like Steve Jobs and Elon Musk, also grew up there.
By 2000, Broadmoor was 68% Black, 26% White and 3% Hispanic – a near mirror image of the city’s racial breakdown.
Green dots galvanize residents into action Isaacson was vacationing in Europe when Katrina hit. Seeing the first TV images of his submerged hometown, he canceled his trip and flew to Baton Rogue, Louisiana. He first saw New Orleans firsthand from inside a helicopter with state leaders as it circled around the devastated city.
Isaacson wept.
“We thought the city would never, ever come back,” he said.
Former Gov. Kathleen Blanco appointed Isaacson to help lead the Louisiana Recovery Authority, tasked with using federal disaster relief funds to help rebuild the city and state.
At around the same time, New Orleans created its own advisory committee, known as the Bring New Orleans Back Committee, made up of urban planners and architects. The commission released a report showing green dots where they thought low-lying, and generally low-income, neighborhoods should be transformed into parkland rather than be rebuilt – including the Lower Ninth Ward and Broadmoor.
Broadmoor residents mobilized, enraged at the so-called “Green Dot” plan. Residents organized into committees, shared information on securing federal disaster money and started drafting a plan to rebuild. Through the Broadmoor Improvement Association, which had been created before Katrina, leaders were able to lasso disaster funds and rebuild the local library and a community center.
Local activist LaToya Cantrell led the Broadmoor Improvement Association in Katrina’s wake and set up meetings with the city’s Sewerage & Water Board, electrical companies and other agencies. (Years later, Cantrell became the first female mayor in New Orleans’ 300-year history.)
LaToya Cantrell, president of Broadmoor Improvement Assoc. and future mayor, stands in front of her office in New Orleans in 2010. By Sean Gardner, for USA TODAY When Isaacson’s alma mater, Harvard University, called asking how it could help, he pointed them to Broadmoor. The university began sending urban planning students to help draw up rebuilding plans.
Three months after the 2005 floods receded, Broadmoor held an outdoor cookout, complete with a New Orleans-style brass band, to herald its rebuilding. The message was clear: Broadmoor was not going anywhere.
“It totally galvanized everybody,” Isaacson said of the Green Dot proposal. “It was a very useful thing to happen to Broadmoor.”
Many of Broadmoor’s homes are raised-basement bungalows, so the floodwaters inundated basements but often left the rest of the house unscathed.
Longtime Broadmoor residents Parviz and Teri Mojgani said more than 7 feet of water poured into their basement, ruining thousands of dollars worth of furniture and goods. They were able to move into the upper part of their home while the basement and downstairs were worked on, Teri Mojgani said.
Parviz and Teri Mojgani, longtime Broadmoor residents who returned home and rebuilt after the floods, work in the front yard of their renovated home that was repaired following Katrina. By Jack Gruber, USA TODAY Still, it took more than a decade for all the federal disaster funds to come through and have her home thoroughly renovated.
Teri Mojgani said she was amazed at how the community came together. She and Parviz joined neighborhood groups and helped others return. The neighborhood began to recover, outpacing even the city’s rebuilding.
Today, Broadmoor boasts a tool lending library, community gardens and teams of social workers working to eradicate poverty and improve access to health care.
Working with local churches, the Broadmoor-based nonprofit group Together New Orleans also launched the Community Lighthouse Project, which equips churches and community centers with commercial-scale solar power and back-up battery capacity so residents can ride out disasters. The first project began at Broadmoor Community Church and has spread across the state.
In many ways, the neighborhood is better off than it was pre-Katrina, Teri Mojgani said.
“If one drives through Broadmoor today, it's not much different – and in fact, probably looks a little better – than it did before Katrina,” she said.
Today, Broadmoor is at about 85% of its pre-Katrina population, higher than the 77% for the rest of the city. It is less Black (46%), more White (33%) and four times more Hispanic (12%) than it was before the storm, according to The Data Center.
Taylor, the Xavier student, returned to New Orleans a few months after Katrina to continue her studies. After graduating, she lived in other parts of the city before moving back to Broadmoor in 2010.
Today, she owns the Crazy Waffle Bar, a “mobile waffle boutique,” and helps run a cooperative kitchen with other food entrepreneurs.
Although her neighborhood is mostly back and most houses renovated, Broadmoor feels different than before the storm, Taylor said. For starters, she said, she doesn’t know many of her neighbors, many of whom arrived after the storm.
“Katrina made you come together because you realized you needed people,” Taylor said. “Now that some people have recovered, the idea that you need people and need your neighbors is no longer there.”
Teri Mojgani said she sees Katrina’s scars each time she drives outside of Broadmoor, through the Gentilly or Lower Ninth Ward neighborhoods – scars that will likely always be there.
But New Orleans’ essence remains intact, she said.
In May, she and Parviz attended a memorial service at Dillard University, a historically Black university in New Orleans. Clergy of different religions spoke, followed by musicians pounding traditional bamboula drums and dancers dressed in traditional African attire.
“It was an excellent example of the character of New Orleans,” she said. “That has not disappeared.”
Then, the memorial morphed into a jazz funeral. A jazz band led a second line parade through the hall and out the door, the brassy sounds of the trombone turning a solemn event hopeful.
Jervis is a national correspondent for USA TODAY based in Austin, Texas. Follow him on X: @MrRJervis.
